title: GraphQL Subscriptions: Transport, Pub/Sub, and Scale
summary: A dense field guide to GraphQL subscriptions end to end — the execution model, WebSocket and SSE transports, pub/sub backends, fan-out at scale, failure modes, and the cases where plain polling is the better engineering call.

chapters.title: What a Subscription Actually Is
points: Definition: a subscription is a third GraphQL root operation type alongside query and mutation, declared as `type Subscription` and wired via the schema's `subscription` root.
Key semantic difference: query/mutation resolve once and return one response; a subscription resolves to a long-lived event stream producing many responses over time.
Spec rule: a subscription operation must select exactly ONE root field — multiple root fields is a validation error, because one operation maps to one event source.
Two-phase execution: `CreateSourceEventStream` (subscribe to the source) happens once; `ExecuteSubscriptionEvent` (run the selection set) happens per published event.
The root field returns a source stream value (the event payload); child resolvers execute normally against it, so subscriptions get the same field-level composition as queries.
Example schema: `type Subscription { messageAdded(roomId: ID!): Message! }` — arguments are filter criteria, evaluated once at subscribe time.
Each event produces a full ExecutionResult with `data` and optional `errors`, shaped exactly like a query response for the same selection set.
A field error inside one event does not terminate the stream; only an error during CreateSourceEventStream fails the subscribe.
Subscriptions are pull-from-the-client-side push: the client declares interest once, the server pushes deltas — no request per update.
Anti-pattern: subscription fields named after CRUD (`getUser`) instead of events (`userUpdated`) — the field name should read as a past-tense fact that occurred.
Mutations must not be triggered by subscriptions; subscription resolvers should be side-effect free readers of an event stream.
Mental model: `Subscription` root field = topic name + filter; the selection set = the projection applied to each event.
Distinct from `@defer`/`@stream`: those are incremental delivery within ONE operation's response, not an open-ended event feed.

chapters.title: The Transport Layer: WebSocket vs SSE vs Long Poll
points: GraphQL spec defines execution, NOT transport — how bytes reach the client is entirely a protocol choice layered on top.
WebSocket: full-duplex over a single upgraded TCP connection (HTTP `Upgrade: websocket`, 101 response); client can send new subscribe messages without a new connection.
SSE (Server-Sent Events): unidirectional server-to-client over plain HTTP, `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, auto-reconnect with `Last-Event-ID` built into the browser EventSource API.
HTTP long polling: client issues a request that the server holds open until an event or timeout, then the client immediately reissues — simplest to deploy, highest per-event overhead.
Comparison row — multiplexing: WebSocket multiplexes many subscriptions on one socket; SSE one stream per connection (or one multiplexed via a custom protocol); long poll one request per cycle.
Comparison row — infrastructure friction: SSE and long poll pass through ordinary HTTP proxies, CDNs, and HTTP/2; WebSocket needs proxies configured for the upgrade handshake.
Comparison row — client-to-server messaging: WebSocket yes; SSE no (needs a separate POST channel); long poll only via the next request.
HTTP/2 note: SSE inherits multiplexing from the connection, so the classic '6 connections per origin' browser limit largely disappears — a historical argument for WebSocket that has weakened.
Compression: WebSocket has `permessage-deflate` (per-frame); SSE gets ordinary `Content-Encoding: gzip` over the stream — usually better ratios on repetitive JSON.
Heartbeats are mandatory in both: SSE sends `:` comment lines; WebSocket sends Ping/Pong frames — without them, load balancers silently drop idle connections (typical idle timeout 60s).
Practical default: if clients only consume events, choose SSE — one less protocol, works with existing HTTP auth, tracing, and logging.
Choose WebSocket when: many concurrent subscriptions per client, low-latency bidirectional needs, or you already run a socket layer.
Serverless caveat: WebSocket needs a connection registry (e.g. API Gateway connection IDs) because no single process owns the socket across invocations.

chapters.title: Wire Protocols: graphql-transport-ws and graphql-sse
points: `graphql-ws` (the `graphql-transport-ws` subprotocol) is the modern standard; `subscriptions-transport-ws` (`graphql-ws` subprotocol name) is deprecated and unmaintained — do not start new work on it.
Subprotocol negotiation happens in the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header; mismatched names between client and server is the #1 cause of silent connection failure.
Message types in graphql-transport-ws: `ConnectionInit`, `ConnectionAck`, `Subscribe`, `Next`, `Error`, `Complete`, `Ping`, `Pong`.
Handshake: client sends `ConnectionInit` (with auth payload) and must receive `ConnectionAck` before sending `Subscribe`; server closes with code 4400/4401 on protocol or auth violation.
Every `Subscribe` carries a client-chosen `id`; all `Next`/`Error`/`Complete` messages echo that id — this is how one socket multiplexes many subscriptions.
`Error` terminates that subscription id; `Complete` is the clean end and may be sent by either side (client sends it to unsubscribe).
Close codes carry meaning: 4400 bad request, 4401 unauthorized, 4409 subscriber-already-exists for a duplicate id, 4408 connection-init timeout.
`graphql-sse` has two modes: 'distinct connections' (one HTTP stream per operation, stateless, CDN-friendly) and 'single connection' (a reservation stream plus separate POSTs).
In graphql-sse the `event:` field is `next` / `complete`, with the ExecutionResult JSON in `data:` — trivially inspectable with `curl -N`.
Queries and mutations can also travel over these protocols — graphql-ws executes them as single `Next` + `Complete` — but you rarely want that; keep them on plain HTTP for caching.
Debug tip: `wscat -c ws://host/graphql -s graphql-transport-ws` then paste the JSON messages by hand to isolate server-side from client-library bugs.
Protocol-level keepalive: graphql-ws Ping/Pong is application-level and survives layers that strip WebSocket control frames.
Versioning gotcha: the deprecated library's subprotocol string is literally `graphql-ws`, which collides with the *package* name of the modern one — read the subprotocol, not the package.

chapters.title: Server-Side Mechanics: Resolvers and PubSub
points: A subscription resolver is a pair: a `subscribe` function returning an AsyncIterable, and an optional `resolve` function mapping each raw event to the field value.
Default behavior: with no `resolve`, the raw published payload must be an object keyed by the subscription field name — a very common source of `null` results.
Minimal shape: `subscribe: () => pubsub.asyncIterableIterator('MESSAGE_ADDED')`, `resolve: (payload) => payload.message`.
Publishing happens in the mutation: `await pubsub.publish('MESSAGE_ADDED', { message })` — the mutation is the write path, the subscription only reads.
Filtering with `withFilter(asyncIteratorFn, (payload, args, context) => boolean)` — runs per event per subscriber, so it must be cheap and synchronous where possible.
Topic granularity beats filtering: publish to `MESSAGE_ADDED:${roomId}` so the broker does the routing, instead of fanning every message to every subscriber to be discarded.
The AsyncIterable contract: `next()` yields events, `return()` runs on unsubscribe — that's where you MUST release broker subscriptions and timers.
Cleanup leak: forgetting `return()`/teardown means a dead client keeps a Redis channel subscription alive forever — memory grows monotonically.
`context` for subscriptions is built at connection time (from `ConnectionInit` payload), not per-event — long-lived contexts hold stale auth and stale DataLoaders.
Never reuse a request-scoped DataLoader across a subscription's lifetime: its cache never invalidates, so subscribers see frozen data forever.
Payload strategy — thin event: publish only IDs, re-fetch in the resolver so every subscriber sees authorized, current data (costs N queries per event).
Payload strategy — fat event: publish the full object, zero re-fetch, but risks leaking fields a given subscriber isn't allowed to see.
Backpressure: an AsyncIterable that ignores consumer speed buffers unboundedly; bound the queue and drop-or-disconnect slow consumers.
Testing: subscription resolvers are testable without sockets — call `subscribe`, publish, and assert on the yielded ExecutionResults.

chapters.title: Pub/Sub Backends: In-Memory, Redis, Kafka, Postgres
points: The in-memory `PubSub` from graphql-subscriptions is a single-process EventEmitter — explicitly documented as unsuitable for production, and it silently breaks the moment you run two replicas.
Failure mode: with N pods behind a load balancer, a mutation hitting pod A never reaches subscribers on pod B — updates appear to work only ~1/N of the time.
Redis Pub/Sub (`graphql-redis-subscriptions`): fire-and-forget fan-out, at-most-once delivery, no persistence — an event published while a subscriber is reconnecting is lost forever.
Redis requires TWO clients: one in subscriber mode (a subscribed connection can't run other commands) and one for publishing.
Redis Streams / Redis 7 alternative: gives persistence and consumer groups, so a reconnecting client can replay from an ID — at the cost of managing trimming.
Kafka: durable, partitioned, replayable log with ordering guaranteed per partition; the right choice when events are also a system-of-record and consumers need offsets.
Kafka trade-off: consumer-group rebalancing and partition assignment make per-user ephemeral topics impractical — subscribe broadly, filter at the gateway.

Postgres `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` (`graphql-postgres-subscriptions`): zero new infrastructure, transactional (notification fires on commit), but payload capped at 8000 bytes and no delivery guarantee if nobody is listening.
NATS / NATS JetStream: lightweight subject-based routing with wildcards (`room.*.message`), optional persistence in JetStream — good middle ground.
Comparison row — delivery guarantee: in-memory none, Redis Pub/Sub at-most-once, Redis Streams / Kafka / JetStream at-least-once with replay.
Comparison row — event ordering: Kafka per-partition, Redis per-channel best-effort, Postgres per-connection commit order.
Change-data-capture pattern: Debezium/logical replication turns table writes into events, so subscriptions can't drift from the database — no forgotten `publish` call.
Choosing rule: correctness need drives the pick — if a missed event is merely a stale UI until refresh, Redis is fine; if it's a lost financial state change, use a durable log.
Idempotency: at-least-once backends WILL redeliver, so events need a stable id and clients must dedupe.

chapters.title: Authentication, Authorization, and Multi-Tenancy
points: The socket is authenticated once, but authorization must be checked continuously — permissions revoked mid-stream do not close the socket by themselves.
Browsers cannot set custom headers on a WebSocket handshake — no `Authorization: Bearer` — so tokens travel in the `ConnectionInit` payload instead.
Never put a token in the WebSocket URL query string: URLs land in proxy logs, access logs, and browser history.
`onConnect` returns the context: validate the token there, throw to reject the handshake, and return the resolved identity as context for all subsequent operations.
Token expiry problem: a JWT valid at connect time may be expired an hour later while the stream is still open — schedule a server-side timer to close the socket at `exp`.
Reauthentication pattern: allow a client-sent message that supplies a refreshed token and updates the connection context in place.
Per-event authorization: for fat payloads, re-check the subscriber's right to see the object at delivery time, not just at subscribe time.
Multi-tenancy: bake the tenant id into the topic name, never rely solely on a filter predicate — a filter bug leaks cross-tenant data, a wrong topic just returns nothing.
CSRF: WebSocket handshakes are not protected by CORS, so validate the `Origin` header server-side explicitly.
Cookie auth over WebSocket works (cookies ARE sent on the handshake) and dodges the header problem, but then Origin checking is mandatory.
Rate limiting must move from requests to connections: cap subscriptions-per-connection, connections-per-user, and events-per-second-per-subscriber.
Query cost limits apply to subscriptions with a multiplier: a depth-5 subscription selection set executes on EVERY event, so its true cost is cost × event rate.
Denial-of-wallet risk: an attacker opening thousands of cheap subscriptions to a high-volume topic converts your fan-out into your bill.

chapters.title: Scaling: Fan-Out, Sticky State, and Cost
points: The core scaling number is fan-out: one publish × N subscribers = N executions of the selection set and N serializations — CPU grows with subscribers, not with writes.
Every open subscription is server state: a socket file descriptor, a broker subscription, and the parsed/validated document — budget roughly tens of KB per connection.
Connection ceiling: OS file descriptor limits (`ulimit -n`) and ephemeral port exhaustion on the proxy tier bite long before application CPU does.
Load balancers must be configured for long-lived connections: raise idle timeout above your heartbeat interval, and never terminate connections on a routine config reload.
Deployments are the hidden pain: every rolling deploy disconnects 100% of subscribers, which then reconnect simultaneously — a self-inflicted thundering herd.
Fix for reconnect storms: jittered exponential backoff on the client, plus a connection-drain window that staggers disconnects during deploys.
Dedicated subscription tier: split the WebSocket gateway from the query API so a socket-heavy workload doesn't starve request/response latency, and so they scale independently.
Sticky sessions are NOT required if the broker delivers to every node — every node subscribes to the topic and pushes to the sockets it happens to hold.
Autoscaling on CPU misleads: subscription nodes are memory- and connection-bound, so scale on connection count and scale in only after draining.
Dedupe identical subscriptions: if 10,000 clients subscribe to the same topic with an identical document, execute once and broadcast the serialized result.
Live queries as an alternative: the client declares data, the server diffs and pushes changes — simpler client code, far more server work to compute diffs.
Federation reality: subscriptions in a federated graph are resolved by one subgraph and proxied by the router; you cannot fan a single subscription across subgraphs.
Observability metrics to track: open connections, subscriptions per connection, events published vs delivered, delivery latency p99, and unsubscribe/teardown rate.
Cost math example: 50k subscribers × 1 event/sec × 2KB payload ≈ 100 MB/s egress — bandwidth, not compute, is often the binding constraint.

chapters.title: Client-Side: Caching, Reconnects, and Missed Events
points: The client wiring is a split link: route operations to the WebSocket/SSE transport when the operation is a subscription, and to HTTP otherwise.
Apollo pattern: `split(({query}) => { const d = getMainDefinition(query); return d.kind === 'OperationDefinition' && d.operation === 'subscription' }, wsLink, httpLink)`.
Normalized cache updates automatically ONLY when the event returns an existing entity's `id` plus changed fields — same-id merge is the whole mechanism.
Additions need explicit cache work: a new list item requires an `updateQuery`/cache modifier, because the cache cannot guess which lists it belongs to.
Deletion is worse: an event announcing a removal must evict the entity AND filter it out of every cached list that referenced it.
`subscribeToMore` attaches an event stream to an existing query so the initial fetch and the live updates share one cache entry and one loading state.
The gap problem: events published between the initial query's snapshot and the subscription becoming active are lost — the UI silently misses updates.
Correct order: open the subscription FIRST, buffer arriving events, then run the initial query, then apply the buffer — subscribe-then-fetch, never fetch-then-subscribe.
Reconnect recovery: on resume, refetch the base query rather than assuming the stream was continuous; treat every reconnect as a possible data gap.
Resumable streams: send a cursor/`Last-Event-ID` on reconnect and have the server replay from it — only possible with a durable pub/sub backend.
Out-of-order and duplicate events happen with at-least-once delivery; carry a monotonic version or timestamp per entity and drop stale writes.
Optimistic UI collision: a local optimistic mutation result plus the server's own subscription echo can double-apply — dedupe on entity id and version.
React Strict Mode double-invokes effects in development, which opens and closes subscriptions twice — verify teardown actually runs before blaming the server.

chapters.title: When Polling Beats a Subscription
points: Default position: polling is the correct choice more often than teams assume — subscriptions buy latency and pay in permanent operational complexity.
Latency arithmetic: a 5-second poll has a 2.5s average staleness; if the product tolerates that, subscriptions add zero user-visible value.
Request math: 1,000 users polling every 10s = 100 requests/sec — trivially absorbed by a cached HTTP endpoint that a CDN can serve.
Poll strengths: stateless, cacheable, load-balanced by default, survives deploys and network changes, debuggable with `curl` and standard access logs.
Conditional requests make polling nearly free: `ETag`/`If-None-Match` returning `304 Not Modified` means no body, no rendering, no serialization on unchanged data.
Poll when the update rate is LOW relative to poll interval — subscribing to something that changes twice a day means holding a connection open all day for two events.
Poll when the consumer count is HUGE and the audience is anonymous — a CDN-cached poll response scales to millions where sockets do not.
Subscribe when the update rate is high AND the freshness requirement is sub-second: chat, collaborative cursors, live trading prices, multiplayer state.
Subscribe when events are irregular and rare-but-urgent: an alert, a completed long-running job — polling wastes requests waiting for a moment that may never come.
Middle ground — smart polling: poll fast when the tab is focused, slow when backgrounded, stop entirely on `document.hidden`; often cuts 80% of traffic.
Middle ground — the notify-then-fetch pattern: use a lightweight subscription that carries only 'something changed', then let the client refetch through the normal cached query path.
Middle ground — SSE-only broadcast: for one-way public data (scores, statuses), a plain SSE endpoint outside GraphQL avoids the whole subscription protocol stack.
Decision rule of thumb: if `time_between_events > poll_interval`, poll; if `events_per_minute > 6` per subscriber and freshness matters, subscribe.
Honest cost comparison: polling costs predictable bandwidth; subscriptions cost engineering time in reconnect logic, broker ops, deploy handling, and cache reconciliation.

chapters.title: Gotchas, Testing, and the Decision Summary
points: Gotcha: mutation publishes before the transaction commits, so subscribers refetch and read pre-commit state — always publish AFTER commit, ideally via a transactional outbox.
Gotcha: subscribing to a topic on every request instead of once per connection multiplies broker subscriptions until the broker's client limit is hit.
Gotcha: no `resolve` function plus a payload not keyed by the field name yields `data: { messageAdded: null }` with no error — the classic silent failure.
Gotcha: unbounded event rate on a hot topic pins the server on JSON serialization; throttle or batch events server-side before delivery.
Gotcha: N+1 inside a subscription resolver runs on every single event, not once per request — the query load is multiplied by event rate × subscriber count.
Gotcha: error inside one event's execution silently terminates the whole stream in some server implementations — catch and emit as a payload-level error instead.
Gotcha: subscriptions are invisible to HTTP-based tooling — APM traces, request logs, and status-code dashboards all show nothing while sockets misbehave.
Testing locally: `wscat` for the raw protocol, `curl -N -H 'Accept: text/event-stream'` for SSE — never debug through the UI first.
Load testing needs connection-oriented tools (k6 with the websockets module, Artillery) because request-per-second benchmarks measure the wrong thing entirely.
Integration test pattern: subscribe, trigger the mutation, assert on the first N yielded results with a timeout — and assert that teardown released the broker subscription.
Chaos check worth running: kill a broker node and confirm subscribers reconnect and resync rather than sitting silently connected to nothing.
Summary — pick transport: SSE by default, WebSocket when bidirectional or heavily multiplexed, long poll only for legacy constraints.
Summary — pick backend: in-memory for a single dev process only; Redis for ephemeral UI freshness; Kafka/JetStream when events must be durable and replayable.
Summary — the three rules: publish thin events after commit, authorize per event and not just at connect, and always assume the client missed something and can resync.
Summary — final judgment: reach for a subscription only when sub-second freshness is a real product requirement; otherwise poll with ETags and spend the complexity budget elsewhere.
